processing: Tea stems, separated from the leaf after steaming, rolling and drying, are sorted and roasted by direct fire, hot sand or far-infrared heat, from a light to a deep roast.
harvest_season: Made all year from stored stems; top grades use stems from first-flush spring tea.
appearance_dry: Short, plump, light golden-brown stems, darker with a deeper roast.
taste_profile: Clean, toasty and gently sweet, with little bitterness. Light roasts keep more umami, deeper ones more roast and sweetness.

brewing.notes: Boiling water and a short steep. It also cold-brews well: about 4 tablespoons to a litre, three hours in the fridge.

vintage_note: Sold as a non-vintage roasted tea, year-round, usually labelled by roast depth and grade rather than harvest. Roasted aroma fades, so buy recently roasted packs and finish them within a couple of months of opening.
description:
Kaga bocha is Ishikawa's roasted stem tea, a kind of hojicha made from stalks rather than leaf. It is the everyday tea of the Kanazawa area, and the stem is what makes it distinct: a lighter, sweeter roast than most leaf hojicha.

Stems come from leaf processing: after steaming, rolling and drying, they are sorted out, cleaned of hard leaf and powder, and roasted. Makers use rotating iron drums over flame, hot sand that puffs the stem, or far-infrared ceramic for lighter roasts. A shallow roast tastes more of tea; a deep one tastes more of toast and caramel.

In the cup it is smooth and aromatic with almost no bitterness, so it suits meals and evenings. Boiling water is right, and a short steep of about 25 seconds keeps it clean. Long steeps only flatten it.

Quality follows the stem. First-flush stems are the premium material, unusual for a style that often starts with low-grade leaf. Check roast level and grade, and note that leaf-roasted Kaga hojicha is a different product under a similar name.

If you like it, try Kyo-bancha next for a smokier roasted tea, or a leaf hojicha to see what the stem changes.
history:
Kaga domain encouraged tea-growing during the Edo period, and Ishikawa was a sizeable producer by Meiji. With exports booming, good tea became dear for local people.

In 1902 the Kanazawa tea merchant Hayashiya Shinbei worked out how to use the stems left over from leaf production. Roasted, they gave a fragrant and cheap tea; once the method was made public it spread through the prefecture.

In 1983 Kaga bocha was presented to Emperor Showa on a visit, and the Maruhachi tea firm's first-flush stem tea, developed for that occasion, helped lift its reputation from cheap to refined.
